Here are several strategies an apartment‐building owner or manager can pursue to lower heating costs. Which measures make sense will depend on your building’s age, construction, existing heating system and budget—but most projects pay back over time in energy savings.

1. Improve the Thermal Envelope  
   • Insulation upgrades – add or top‐up insulation in lofts, cavity walls or facades.  
   • Seal air leaks – use weather‐stripping around windows and doors and seal gaps at service penetrations (pipes, cables).  
   • High-performance windows – replace single-glazed sashes with double or triple glazing and low-E coatings.  

2. Optimize the Heating System  
   • Modern boilers or heat pumps – replace an old gas/oil boiler with a high-efficiency condensing boiler or an electrically driven ground‐ or air-source heat pump.  
   • Zoned temperature control – install thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs) or digital room thermostats so you only heat occupied apartments or common areas.

To achieve the greatest reduction in heating costs, you should focus first on minimizing heat losses through the building envelope, then optimize your heating system and controls. Here’s a step-by-step priority list:

1. Improve insulation and airtightness  
   • Roof/attic insulation: Upgrading or topping up insulation here often yields the largest gains per invested krona.  
   • Wall insulation: Cavity-fill or internal/external insulation reduces heat loss through walls.  
   • Floor/crawl-space insulation: Prevents cold from seeping in underfoot.  
   • Draught-proofing and sealing: Seal gaps around windows, doors, service penetrations and junctions to avoid uncontrolled air leakage.

2. Upgrade windows and doors  
   • Install high-performance (e.g. triple-glazed) windows with low-emissivity coatings.  
   • Ensure frames are well sealed and thermally broken.  
   • Consider external or internal shutters/blinds for night-time insulation.

Direct-acting (resistive) electric radiators convert virtually 100 percent of the incoming electrical energy into heat at the point of use. In that sense, they are “fully efficient” as room heaters. However, when assessing overall energy efficiency and running costs, you must consider how the electricity is generated and delivered:

1. Generation and distribution losses  
   – Electricity typically goes through generation (power plant), transmission and distribution networks before reaching your home. Depending on the national grid mix and transmission losses, only 30–50 percent of the primary energy (for instance, the energy in fuel or renewable source) ends up as usable electricity in your radiator.

2. Cost of electricity versus other fuels  
   – In most markets, the kilowatt-hour price for electricity is higher than for natural gas, district heating or heat-pump operation. Even though the radiator itself is 100 percent efficient, the higher per-kWh cost usually makes direct electr

Here are several practical measures you can take to get the most out of direct-acting electric radiators—both in terms of comfort and cost-efficiency:

1. Install programmable or smart thermostats  
   • Set lower temperatures (e.g. 18–19 °C) during sleeping hours or when the home is unoccupied, and raise them only shortly before you return.  
   • Some models can learn your daily routine or be controlled remotely via smartphone.

2. Zone your heating  
   • Divide your home into heating zones (e.g. living area, bedrooms, bathroom) and control each radiator independently.  
   • Only heat the rooms you’re actually using rather than keeping the entire house at the same temperature.

3. Use thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs)  
   • Fitting TRVs lets each radiator maintain its own temperature set-point, avoiding overheating and unnecessary power draw.  
   • You can manually “dial back” radiators in little-used areas (hallways, guest rooms).

Improving the energy efficiency of domestic hot‐water (DHW) systems typically involves a combination of equipment upgrades, better controls, improved insulation and user‐side measures. Even without specific building data, the following strategies are widely applicable:

1. Upgrade the Heat Source  
   • High-efficiency heat pumps  
     – Air-to-water or ground-source heat pumps can achieve coefficients of performance (COP) of 3–4, meaning 1 kW of electricity produces 3–4 kW of heat.  
   • Condensing boilers or water heaters  
     – Condensing gas or oil boilers recover heat from flue gases, boosting efficiency by up to 10–15 % compared with standard units.  
   • Instantaneous (tankless) heaters  
     – Eliminates storage losses but requires proper sizing and good gas/electric supply.

2. Recover and Reuse Waste Heat  
   • Solar thermal collectors  
     – Pre-heat storage tank water using solar energy during sunny months; can meet 50–70 % of annual DHW demand in many climates.

Optimizing domestic hot-water (DHW) production in an apartment building typically involves improving both the generation side (how heat is produced) and the distribution side (how heat is delivered to taps). Below are key strategies to consider:

1. Efficient Heat Generation  
   • High-efficiency heat sources  
     – Modern condensing boilers (natural gas or biofuel) with > 90% seasonal efficiency.  
     – Electric or hybrid heat pumps (air-to-water, ground-to-water) achieving coefficients of performance (COP) of 3–4 or more.  
   • Renewable integration  
     – Solar thermal panels for pre-heating DHW, sized to cover part of annual demand.  
     – Wastewater heat recovery units that capture heat from showers and grey water.  
   • Buffer storage and stratification  
     – Properly sized DHW tanks (buffer cylinders) to decouple production from peak demand.  
     – Internal baffling or stratification plates to maintain temperature layers and minimize mixing losses.

An energy declaration (in Swedish, “energideklaration”) is a standardized report of a building’s energy performance. It is prepared by an accredited energy expert and must be carried out when a building is constructed, sold, let or undergoes major renovation. The key elements of an energy declaration include:

1. Energy Performance Rating  
   – The building is assigned an energy class (A–G), much like appliances or cars, indicating its overall efficiency.  
   – The latest assessment is the one that applies if several declarations exist.

2. Energy Use and Calculations  
   – Measured or calculated annual energy use per square meter heated area (Atemp).  
   – Breakdown of energy consumption by heating, hot water, ventilation, lighting and auxiliary systems.

3. Building Characteristics  
   – Type of building (e.g. detached house, apartment block, school).  
   – Heated floor area (Atemp), number of floors and stairwells.  
   – Construction era, insulation levels and window types.

Energy-efficiency improvement refers to any change or upgrade that reduces a building’s energy consumption while maintaining (or improving) its level of comfort and functionality. In practice, this means making the building “smarter” about how it uses energy and reducing losses. Common measures include:

• Building envelope upgrades  
  – Adding or thickening insulation in walls, roofs and floors  
  – Installing high-performance windows and doors with better seals and lower U-values  
  – Sealing air leaks around joints, penetrations and service entries  

• Heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) improvements  
  – Replacing old boilers, heat pumps or chillers with higher-efficiency models  
  – Upgrading controls (thermostats, zoned heating/ventilation, variable-speed drives)  
  – Balancing airflows and optimizing ventilation rates  

• Lighting and appliance upgrades  
  – Switching to LED or other high-efficacy lighting  
  – Installing occupancy and daylight sensors

1. Space Heating and Cooling (HVAC Systems)  
   • Air‐source or ground‐source heat pumps, electric furnaces and fan coils.

Natural (or passive) ventilation relies on wind and buoyancy forces rather than powered fans or ducts. Compared with fully mechanical ventilation systems, it offers several advantages:

1. Lower Energy Consumption  
   • No or very limited use of electric fans, reducing operational energy costs.  
   • Contributes to a building’s overall energy performance and can improve its EPC rating.

2. Reduced Operating Costs  
   • Fewer moving parts and no complex air-handling units mean lower maintenance and service expenses.  
   • No recurring costs for fan filters, belts or motor repairs.

3. Simplicity of Installation  
   • Requires fewer components (vents, operable windows, air inlets and outlets).  
   • Can be integrated into the architectural design with minimal ductwork or plantroom space.

4. Improved Indoor Air Quality (IAQ)  
   • Fresh outdoor air enters directly, diluting indoor pollutants and carbon dioxide more naturally.

Optimizing natural ventilation involves both a careful architectural layout and occupant-controlled strategies. Below are key approaches you can employ:

1. Building Orientation and Form  
   • Orient the long façades toward prevailing winds to capture breezes.  
   • Use a narrow floor plan or “slender” building form so that wind can penetrate more easily from one side to the other.  
   • Avoid large obstructions (e.g., high walls or dense landscaping) immediately upwind of windows or vents.

2. Placement and Size of Openings  
   • Provide high and low openings on opposite sides of a room or corridor. Low vents admit cool air, while high vents (clerestory windows, rooflights or ventilators) exhaust warm air via the stack effect.  
   • Aim for a total operable opening area of at least 5 – 10 % of the floor area to ensure sufficient airflow.  
   • Where possible, include adjustable louvres or trickle vents so you can fine-tune airflow rates without fully opening windows.

When you choose household appliances, their own EU energy-label class (A +++ down to G) adds directly to your building’s overall energy performance. In practice, this means:

1. Building energy class as a baseline  
   • A-class buildings (A/A +) already have low heating, cooling and ventilation losses. In such homes, appliances typically become the single largest energy user—so investing in A +++ or A ++ machines makes a noticeable dent in total consumption.  
   • G-class or poorly insulated homes have high envelope losses, so although replacing a refrigerator or washer with a top-class model still saves energy, the percentage reduction of your total bill will be smaller than in an A-class home.

Control and regulation technology (often called control engineering or automation technology) is the discipline and set of tools used to monitor, manage and steer the behavior of technical processes so that they maintain desired operating conditions.  In practice, it involves:

• Sensors and Measurement  
  – Devices that continuously register process variables (temperature, pressure, flow, level, speed, humidity, etc.)  
• Controllers and Algorithms  
  – Logic or mathematical models (from simple on/off relays to PID controllers and advanced model-based regulators) that compare measured values with set-points and calculate corrective actions  
• Actuators and Final Elements  
  – Equipment (valves, dampers, motors, pumps, heaters, etc.) that implement the controller’s commands to adjust the process  
• Feedback and Feedforward Loops  
  – Closed-loop (feedback) systems automatically correct deviations by comparing actual and target values; feedforward strategies anticipate disturbance

1. Assess Current Capacity and Requirements

In most building‐lighting standards (for example EN 12464-1 which also informs Swedish practice), general (normal‐use) lighting in stairwells is specified as follows:

• Maintained horizontal illuminance: 100 lux measured at floor level (i.e. the walking plane).  
• Uniformity (Uo = Emin/Eavg): ≥ 0.4 across the walking surface.  
• On the individual stair treads it is good practice to verify that there are no dark spots—measurements should still meet at least 100 lux at 0.2 m above each tread nosing.  

In addition to the normal lighting:

• Emergency/escape‐route lighting must provide a minimum of 1 lux (measured at floor level) continuously along the center line of the escape route in case of power failure.  

Typical recommendations for fixture selection in stairwells also include a colour rendering index (CRI) ≥ 80 and a correlated colour temperature (CCT) in the range 3000–4000 K to ensure good visibility and way‐finding.

In Sweden there is no single “legal” temperature set‐point for stairwells, but both fire-safety and comfort rules in Boverket’s Building Regulations (BBR) and good practice guidelines point to the same general range:

• Recommended temperature: 16 °C – 18 °C  
  – Ensures that the building fabric stays dry (prevents condensation and mould).  
  – Offers safe, comfortable evacuation conditions in an emergency.  

• Minimum allowable temperature: 12 °C – 14 °C  
  – Some housing companies choose to setback to around 12 °C outside core usage hours (nights/weekends) to save energy.  
  – You should not fall below +10 °C long-term, since that risks freeze-damage in pipeways and increased damp.  

If you need to demonstrate compliance in an energy-performance declaration (EPC), simply report the steady-state temperature you maintain in the stairwells—most commonly 17 °C in residential buildings.
